engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: The Fork
chess.body: A fork attacks two pieces simultaneously with one piece. Knight forks are the deadliest — they move in an L-shape and cannot be blocked. Look for squares your knight can reach that simultaneously attack king + queen, or rook + rook. Practice: set up NxC5+ forking king and rook. Classic beginner trap.

book.author: Tim Ferriss
book.chapter: The 80/20 of Everything: Most Effort Is Wasted
book.lesson: Ferriss's most useful contribution: ruthless application of Pareto's 80/20 principle to everything. 20% of customers generate 80% of revenue — and usually 120% of headaches. 20% of tasks generate 80% of results. 20% of foods cause 80% of health problems for a given person. The exercise: list every customer, task, and activity. Identify the 20% producing 80% of value. Do more of that. Then identify the 20% consuming 80% of your time and energy with minimal value. Eliminate, automate, or delegate it. Most knowledge workers are busy with the bottom 80% and neglect the top 20%.
book.key_quote: Being busy is not the same as being productive. Most of what we do doesn't matter nearly as much as we think it does.
book.action: List your 10 most frequent work activities. Rank by impact. The bottom 3 — can any be eliminated, automated, or delegated?
crux: The New Rich optimise for time and mobility, not for accumulation then retirement.
Deferred-life planning is the default and it is a bad plan.
Dreamlining: cost out the specific life you want. It is usually cheaper than assumed.
Relative income (per hour) beats absolute income.
Pareto: 80% of results come from 20% of inputs. Find and cut the rest.
Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available. Short deadlines force focus.
Use both together — do only the important, and give it very little time.
Selective ignorance: a low-information diet is a productivity intervention.
Batch everything. Email, calls, errands. Context switching is the tax.
Automate with clear rules and delegated authority, or you've just added coordination work.
Build a muse: a product with recurring revenue that doesn't need your presence.
Test demand before building anything. Cheap ads before inventory.
Mini-retirements beat one long retirement at the end.
Fear-setting: define the worst case in detail and it usually shrinks.
learnings: Being busy is often a form of avoidance.
Cutting the wrong work beats optimising it.
Deadlines are a focus tool, not just a commitment.
Automation without decision rules just moves the work.
examples: Ferriss cut 98% of his client list, kept the top 5, and income rose while hours dropped from 80 to 15.
BrainQUICKEN was validated with small Google Ads spends before stock was ordered.
Fear-setting a trip to London: worst case listed, all reversible. He went.
adapt: The bots are the muse infrastructure — they run whether you're interviewing or asleep.
80/20 the content: which posts actually drive followers? Cut the rest.
Batch Telegram and email into two windows. This is the same fix Deep Work prescribes.
Fear-set the Dubai move: worst case is a return to KL with more experience. Reversible.

interview_tech.q: What is open-to-buy and why should finance care?
interview_tech.a: Open-to-buy is the budget available to purchase stock for a future period, given planned sales, planned markdowns and target closing stock. It is where merchandise planning and finance meet. Finance should care because it is the single control that prevents over-buying — the root cause of the markdown spiral that destroys gross margin two seasons later. If buyers can commit outside OTB without sign-off, your inventory forecast is decoration.

interview_tech.q: What is the effect of a sale-and-leaseback on your financials?
interview_tech.a: Cash in now, occupancy cost forever. You derecognise the asset, recognise a gain or loss limited to the rights transferred, and recognise a right-of-use asset and lease liability under IFRS 16 — so leverage does not fall by the full cash proceeds. It flatters current-year cash and often current-year profit while committing you to rent for 15–20 years. Legitimate for releasing capital from non-core property; a warning sign when used to plug an operating cash shortfall.

interview_soft.q: Why do you want to be a CFO, and why in retail?
interview_soft.a: Structure: motive, evidence, specificity. Weak answers say 'growth' and 'leadership'. Strong answer names the work: 'I want the seat where capital allocation is decided, not just reported. In FP&A I model the store investment case; the CFO decides which twelve of thirty get built. Retail because the feedback loop is daily — you see whether the decision worked in the sales line the next week, which is not true in most industries.' Then one proof point with a number attached.

interview_soft.q: How do you build a finance team, and how do you handle an underperformer?
interview_soft.a: Building: hire for one clear gap, not a generalist; define what good looks like in writing before the first review, not after. Underperformance: the honest answer is that you probably waited too long once, and learned from it. Structure — early specific feedback with examples, an agreed plan with dates, documented check-ins, and a decision at the end of it either way. The failure mode they are probing for is a manager who avoids the conversation and lets the team carry someone for a year.

cfo_field.q: Learn the lease standard properly. In the Gulf it is not a footnote.
cfo_field.a: IFRS 16 put every store lease on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Two consequences a CFO must be able to say out loud: EBITDA is now flattered, because rent that used to sit in operating costs is split into depreciation and interest; and leverage ratios move even though nothing about the business changed. If your covenant is set on a pre-IFRS-16 basis, know it before the bank asks.

cfo_field.q: Automation without a control map is how a finance function loses its audit trail.
cfo_field.a: Before automating a process, write down: who can initiate, who approves, what the system does without a human, and where the exception report goes. Automation does not remove controls; it moves them from people to configuration, and configuration drifts silently. The question 'what breaks if this runs wrong for a month before anyone notices' is the one that separates a finance automation from a finance incident.

Focus on early queen‑side development: after 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6, play c4 instead of passive moves; aim for c4‑d5 exchange by move 5 to seize central space and prevent Black’s comfortable queen‑side setup.
